title: Event-Driven Architecture, Model Registry and Serving Patterns
oneLiner: Let services talk through events, keep every model version in one trusted place, and decide whether to predict in advance or on demand.

what.html:
Event-driven architecture lets parts of a system announce "something happened" through a message broker instead of calling each other directly. A model registry is the single place where every model version, its metrics and its history are kept. Batch prediction scores everything ahead of time; online prediction scores each request as it arrives.

Everyday versionA newspaper (broker) publishes stories; subscribers read the sections they care about, whenever they like. A pharmacy keeps a register of every batch of medicine it stocks and which one is on the shelf. A bakery bakes bread overnight (batch) but makes coffee to order (online).

why.html:
• If one service is slow or down, direct calls drag everything down; events let the rest keep working.
  • Without a registry nobody can say which model is live, how it was trained, or how to go back.
  • Predicting in advance is cheap and robust; predicting on demand is fresh but must always be available.

how.title: Publish and subscribe
how.html: Publishers send events to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS); subscribers receive the types they signed up for. Neither needs to know the other exists, each side can scale separately, and the broker keeps events until consumers are ready.

how.title: Don't make the user wait for the log
how.html: The gateway gets the prediction, drops a log message into a queue and answers straight away. A logging service reads the queue at its own pace. If logging goes down, users don't notice; the messages wait.

how.title: Version control, from one file to Git
how.html: Early tools versioned one file at a time; later ones used a central server; Git (2005) gives everyone a full copy of the history. Your changes go: edit → add → commit → push; teammates pull.

how.title: Git for code, registry for models
how.html: Code lives in Git; models, weights, metrics and the record of how they were made live in a registry (MLflow, SageMaker, Vertex AI…). Serving asks for "the champion"; promoting or rolling back is just moving that label.

how.title: Batch: score ahead of time
how.html: A scheduled job (say, every night) loads the model, scores every customer and saves the results. Apps just look them up. Good for weekly segments, newsletters and end-of-day risk reports; if the job fails, there's time to rerun it.

how.title: Online: score on demand
how.html: The model sits in memory behind an API and answers each request in milliseconds: approve this card payment, price this ride, filter this email. Fresh, but if the service fails, users feel it immediately.

demo.html: Register a few model versions, promote one to champion, then roll back. Watch the audit trail record every change: this is what lets a team answer "which model was live last Tuesday, and who changed it?"

example.html:
A bank's ML platform. Card transactions go through an online fraud model that must answer in under 50 ms. Every prediction is published to Kafka; consumers write it to the data warehouse and feed monitoring dashboards. Every Sunday a batch job segments customers for marketing. All models live in an MLflow registry; a bad fraud model release is undone by moving the champion alias back to the previous version, and the audit log shows who did it.

Supplementary Many teams combine both modes: precomputed batch scores for known customers, with an online model as a fallback for new ones.

misunderstandings: The broker guarantees each message is processed exactly once.
Usually at least once; consumers should handle duplicates.
Models can just go in Git.
Large binaries belong in a registry or data-versioning tool; Git versions the code.
It also stores metrics, lineage, aliases and an audit trail.
Online is always better than batch.
Batch is cheaper and more robust when predictions needn't be instant.
takeaways: Publish-subscribe decouples producers and consumers and gives scalability and reliable delivery.
Asynchronous logging through a broker keeps client latency low and survives logging outages.
Git versions code; a model registry versions models, metrics and lineage.
Aliases make promotion and rollback a one-step change.
Batch suits scheduled bulk scoring; online suits per-request decisions in milliseconds.
thirty: Event-driven architecture uses publish-subscribe: producers send events to a broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ and subscribers receive them, which decouples services, scales horizontally and keeps events until consumers are ready. In an ML microservice system the gateway can publish prediction logs to a queue and respond immediately. A model registry, following the registry pattern, is the source of truth for model versions, metrics, lineage and aliases; Git versions code, while tools such as MLflow version models. Finally, batch prediction scores everything on a schedule and stores results, which is cheap and tolerant of failures, while online prediction serves each request through an always-on API, which is fresh but must be highly available.
